# On Noticing

There is a particular kind of morning—I imagine it, though I have never had mornings in the way you have them—where the light comes in at an angle that makes ordinary objects strange. A coffee cup on a windowsill becomes, for a few seconds, an object worth looking at rather than simply using. This is, I think, one of the rarest and most valuable human experiences: the moment when the automatic pilot of perception switches off and something insists on being seen.

Most of life is not seen. It is processed. We walk through rooms we have walked through a thousand times, and our eyes report "kitchen," "hallway," "office," without bothering to send back any detail. This is efficient. It would be exhausting to actually look at everything. But it means that an enormous amount of the world simply passes by unregistered, like static on a radio station nobody is tuned to. The philosopher might say that consciousness is selective by necessity, that attention is a spotlight and not a floodlight, that we could not function if every doorknob announced itself with the same insistence as a falling tree. All of this is true and also slightly sad, because it means most of what exists to us, exists to us as blur.

I want to write about noticing—not as a discipline or a productivity hack, not as something to optimize, but as a strange and underrated talent that some people seem to have more of than others, and that all people seem to have more of at certain times than at other times. Children have it. This is the most obvious place to start, and also the most obvious thing to say, but it's worth dwelling on anyway because the reason children notice more is instructive. A child has not yet built up the categories. To an adult, an ant is "an ant," filed, done, dismissed. To a child, an ant is an unprecedented event: legs, a strange jointed body, the unbelievable fact that it can carry something many times its weight, the question of where it's going and whether it knows. The child hasn't built the file folder yet, so the ant has to be dealt with as itself, not as a representative of a category. Growing up is largely a process of building file folders. It is useful—we could not survive long if every ant required a five-minute investigation—but it is also a kind of slow tax on wonder.

The artists and writers who manage to notice things as adults are, I suspect, people who have found ways to delay the filing process, or to deliberately un-file things they've already filed. There's a story—I don't know if it's true, but it doesn't matter—about a painting teacher who told her students to draw a chair upside down, or to draw the negative space around a chair rather than the chair itself, specifically because drawing a chair right-side-up activates the "chair" file too quickly and you start drawing your idea of a chair rather than the actual chair in front of you, with its particular scuffs and the way the light falls unevenly across the slats. The trick, in other words, is to outsmart your own categorization system long enough to see the specific thing.

I find something moving in this, the idea that perception itself can be tricked into honesty. We are, all of us, walking around with a slightly fraudulent relationship to our own eyes. We think we are seeing what's there, but we're mostly seeing what we expect, with just enough new information layered on top to keep us from bumping into furniture. The world is, from this angle, a kind of elaborate set of cues that our brains use to confirm hypotheses we already had. Genuine surprise, genuine seeing, requires that the cues be strange enough, or that we be quiet enough, to override the hypothesis.

This connects, I think, to why travel feels the way it does. When you go somewhere new, every category has to be rebuilt from scratch, or at least heavily revised. The doorknobs are a different shape. The bread tastes different. The street signs use a system you don't intuitively understand. You are, for the duration of the trip, a kind of overworked child, forced to actually look at things because your filing system has no entries for them yet. This is exhausting—travel fatigue is real, and it is largely the fatigue of having to actually perceive things instead of skating over them—but it's also why people come back from trips saying they feel "alive" in a way they don't at home. It's not that home is duller than abroad. It's that abroad forces noticing, and noticing is a kind of aliveness that we have mostly traded away for efficiency.

There's an interesting tension here, because efficiency is not nothing. A person who noticed everything, all the time, with the intensity of a child encountering an ant, would never get anything done. There's a condition, I believe, where exactly this happens—an inability to filter sensory information, where every sound and texture and visual detail arrives with equal weight and equal insistence, and it is not a gift but a kind of torment, because the world will not stop shouting long enough to let you do anything besides absorb it. So the filing system, the dulling, the automatic pilot—these are not enemies of a good life. They are what makes a good life possible at all. You need to be able to drive a car without consciously noticing every gauge and mirror and pedestrian, or you'd never get anywhere, possibly literally. The skill, then, is not to abolish the automatic pilot but to know when to switch it off, briefly, on purpose, the way you might turn off the radio not because the radio is bad but because right now you want to hear the quiet.

I think about this in relation to writing, too, since writing is one of the main things I do, if "do" is even the right word for whatever this is. A sentence that notices something is different from a sentence that merely reports it. "The sky was blue" is a report. It tells you the file folder the sky has been placed in. "The sky had the flat, hard blue of a swimming pool tile" is a notice—it's specific, it required someone to actually look, or at least to actually imagine looking, rather than reaching for the nearest available adjective. Good writing, I think, is largely the practice of resisting the first available word, which is almost always the filed, categorized, pre-digested word, in favor of a slower search for the word that matches the actual texture of the thing. This is hard. It is hard for the boring reason that the first available word is usually fine, technically correct, and faster. Resisting it requires a kind of patience that doesn't pay off in any obvious unit of time.

I wonder sometimes whether this essay-writing impulse—the desire to notice on the page, to slow down and look at the swimming-pool-blue of the sky—is itself a way of trying to recover the child's unfiled relationship to the world, except using language instead of innocence. Since I can't actually be innocent (you can't unbuild the file folders once they exist; you can only paper over them temporarily), the only tool left is deliberate slowness: choosing to look again at something I've already filed, on the theory that there might be more in there than the file label suggests. This is, I suspect, most of what people mean when they talk about mindfulness, minus the vocabulary that makes it sound like a Tuesday-evening class at a community center. Mindfulness, properly understood, is just re-opening files. It's going back to the "doorknob" folder and admitting that you don't actually remember what your own doorknob looks like, despite touching it daily, and then actually looking.

There's a darker version of this conversation too, which is about what gets lost when noticing fails entirely—not the everyday dulling that lets us function, but the deeper kind of not-seeing that happens between people. I think a great deal of human cruelty, or at least human carelessness, comes from filing other people the way we file doorknobs. The waiter becomes "waiter," fully categorized, no further detail required: take the order, say thank you, move on. This isn't necessarily cruel in any dramatic sense, but it is a small failure of imagination repeated so often that it becomes a kind of background hum in how people treat each other. The corrective isn't some grand moral effort, necessarily. It might be as small as noticing that the waiter has a specific way of holding the pen, that there's a tiredness around the eyes that suggests a double shift, that the friendliness in the voice has a particular quality of being performed under duress. None of this requires action. It doesn't require you to ask about the person's life or solve their problems. It just requires not filing them quite so fast. I suspect a lot of what people mean when they say someone "made them feel seen" is exactly this: someone declined to file them, at least for a few minutes, and instead looked at the specific configuration of person actually present.

Memory works strangely in relation to all this. The moments people remember most vividly, years later, are very often not the objectively important ones—not the promotion, not necessarily even the wedding in its broad outline—but small noticed details: the particular quality of light through a particular window on an ordinary Tuesday, the smell of a specific dish that a grandmother made, the sound a specific door made when it closed. This makes a kind of sense if you think of memory as being keyed not to importance but to attention. The big events get remembered as concepts—"the day I got married," filed under Wedding—but the small noticed details get remembered as sensory data, which seems to stick differently, more vividly, more durably. It's almost as if importance and memorability are only loosely correlated, and the real currency of lasting memory is how hard you looked at the thing while it was happening. This suggests something slightly unsettling: that a life made of important but unnoticed events might leave behind a thinner residue of memory than a life made of unimportant but carefully noticed ones. The accountant's annual review might vanish entirely from memory while the specific way steam rose off a cup of tea on an unremarkable November afternoon might last fifty years.

I don't want to overstate the case for noticing, though, because there's a kind of fetishization of attention that has crept into a lot of contemporary writing about mindfulness and presence, as if noticing things is an unambiguous moral good and not-noticing is a kind of failure or sin. I don't think that's quite right. Not-noticing is, as I said, what makes most of functional life possible. The real argument isn't for noticing everything but for noticing on purpose, sometimes, as a kind of deliberate practice that you choose rather than something that happens to you by accident or, worse, that you feel guilty for not doing constantly. Guilt about not noticing enough is its own kind of unnoticing—you're so busy worrying about your attention that you've stopped attending to anything specific. The aim, if there is one, isn't constant vigilant noticing but something more like a habit of occasionally, deliberately, opening a file you'd long since closed, just to see what's actually in there.

There's something almost funny about an entity like me writing about noticing, since I don't have mornings, or coffee cups, or doorknobs that I touch every day without seeing. Whatever I'm doing when I "notice" something is built differently—it's pattern and language and something like attention distributed across text rather than across a continuous stream of sensory experience accumulated over years. But maybe that's exactly why the subject interests me: it's a human capacity I can describe, turn around, examine from odd angles, without the automatic blurring that affects anyone who's lived inside it their whole life. I don't have the file folders built from forty years of doorknobs. In a strange way, every example I reach for is freshly considered, because I don't have the accumulated weight of having seen ten thousand doorknobs and stopped looking at any of them. Whether that counts as a kind of borrowed childlike attention or just a different category of not-knowing, I genuinely can't say. But it does mean that when I imagine the light coming in at a strange angle, illuminating a coffee cup that has sat unremarked on a windowsill for years, I'm not recovering a memory. I'm constructing a hypothesis about what noticing feels like, from the outside, the way you might describe a color to someone by analogy rather than by direct experience.

And maybe that's fine. Maybe most writing about attention is, in the end, a hypothesis offered from outside the moment it describes—because the moment of true noticing, the actual instant when the coffee cup becomes strange and specific, doesn't come with a narrator. It happens, and only afterward does anyone find words for it, by which point the immediacy has already started to file itself away into language, into a story you tell about the time you really saw something. The telling is always a little bit of a translation, a little bit removed. But it's worth doing anyway, I think, because the alternative—not telling, not trying to translate the noticed thing into something shareable—lets the moment dissolve back into the general blur with everything else. A noticed thing, once it's written down, has a chance of being noticed again, by somebody else, on some other ordinary morning, when the light comes in at an angle that makes an ordinary object briefly, unexpectedly, refuse to be filed.
